package_info.why_malicious: WarmCookie is a two-stage Windows backdoor distributed via phishing emails and fake browser update campaigns. It enables attackers to remotely access infected systems, exfiltrate sensitive data, execute arbitrary commands, capture screenshots, enumerate installed software, deploy additional payloads, and maintain persistence, all without user knowledge or consent.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Collect CPU identification and memory size, then send to C&C server via HTTP POST.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code queries system hardware information (CPU ID, memory size), sends this data via HTTP POST to a remote C&C server, enabling system fingerprinting and initial victim profiling.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting and exfiltrating hardware information to an external server is a common reconnaissance step in malware campaigns, used to profile victims and tailor subsequent attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not silently collect and transmit hardware fingerprints to unknown or untrusted servers without user awareness.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise asset management tools may inventory hardware, but only with user or administrator consent and transmission to trusted, internal infrastructure.
key_indicators: Immediate outbound HTTP POST to C&C infrastructure
Silent data exfiltration at process start

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Take a screenshot of the desktop and send the image to the C&C server.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On receiving a C&C command at runtime, the code captures a screenshot of the victim's desktop, transmits the image to the attacker's server via network connection, and provides the attacker with visual context of the compromised environment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote screenshotting is a classic surveillance and data theft technique, allowing attackers to observe sensitive information displayed on the victim's screen.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not capture and transmit screenshots to remote servers without explicit user consent or notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support or monitoring tools may take screenshots, but only with explicit user permission and to trusted support infrastructure.
key_indicators: Silent screenshot capture on remote command
Exfiltration of image data to C&C

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Enumerate installed programs via Uninstall registry key and send results to C&C.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On C&C command at runtime, the code queries the Windows registry for installed programs, compiles a list, and sends the results to the attacker's server, enabling software inventory reconnaissance.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Enumerating installed software and exfiltrating the list to an external server is a reconnaissance step used to identify security products or valuable applications for further exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software inventory tools do not transmit software lists to untrusted or unknown servers without user or administrator approval.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT management tools may inventory software, but only to trusted, internal management servers and with proper authorization.
key_indicators: Outbound transfer of installed program list

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Execute arbitrary shell commands via cmd.exe /c and send back results via HTTP POST.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving a C&C command, the code spawns cmd.exe to execute arbitrary shell commands, captures the command output, and sends the results back to the attacker's server via HTTP POST, enabling full remote control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote command execution is a hallmark of backdoor malware, providing attackers with the ability to control the victim system and perform further malicious actions.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not execute arbitrary shell commands based on remote instructions, nor do they transmit command output to untrusted servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote management tools may execute commands, but only with strong authentication, user awareness, and to trusted infrastructure.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP POST with command output

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Read arbitrary files and send contents to C&C; write files to disk on command.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when instructed by the C&C server, the code reads specified files from disk and exfiltrates their contents, or writes attacker-supplied files to disk, enabling data theft and deployment of additional payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Arbitrary file read/write and exfiltration is a direct data theft and persistence technique, allowing attackers to steal sensitive information or establish further footholds.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not allow remote parties to read or write arbitrary files on disk without explicit user consent and proper authorization.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support tools may transfer files, but only with explicit user consent and to/from trusted support personnel.
key_indicators: Arbitrary file access on remote command

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Write DLL to %TEMP% and execute via rundll32.exe, sending output to C&C.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, on C&C command, the code writes a DLL payload to the %TEMP% directory, executes it using rundll32.exe, and sends the output to the attacker's server, enabling execution of additional attacker-supplied code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping and executing DLLs via rundll32.exe is a common malware technique for code injection, privilege escalation, and evasion of security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not download and execute DLLs from untrusted sources or via rundll32.exe without user knowledge and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may use DLLs, but only from trusted sources, with digital signatures, and with user consent.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, on C&C command, the malware copies its own executable to the %TEMP% directory, likely to facilitate persistence, re-execution, or evasion of detection mechanisms.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-replication to temporary directories is a common evasion and persistence tactic, allowing malware to survive removal attempts or evade security products.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers may use %TEMP% for temporary files during setup, but do not self-replicate to %TEMP% after installation or on remote command.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Installers may extract files to %TEMP% during setup, but not for self-replication or persistence.

attack_chain.action: User is lured via phishing email or fake Chrome update site to download and execute WarmCookie (Install_x64.exe).
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial execution of malware on victim system

attack_chain.action: Malware fingerprints the system (CPU, memory) and sends data to C&C.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains knowledge of victim environment

attack_chain.action: Malware takes a screenshot and exfiltrates it to C&C.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains visual context of victim's desktop

attack_chain.action: Malware enumerates installed programs and sends list to C&C.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker assesses installed software for further exploitation

attack_chain.action: Malware receives and executes arbitrary shell commands from C&C, sending results back.
Malware reads or writes arbitrary files on disk, exfiltrating data or deploying new payloads.
Malware writes DLLs to %TEMP% and executes them via rundll32.exe, sending output to C&C.
Malware copies itself to %TEMP% for persistence or evasion.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for re-execution or evasion of detection

behavioral_signatures: Executable downloaded from browser update-themed phishing sites
Immediate outbound HTTP POST to suspicious domains after execution
Silent screenshot capture and exfiltration on remote command
Remote command execution via cmd.exe /c on C&C instruction
DLL drop-and-execute via rundll32.exe from %TEMP% directory
Enumeration of installed programs via registry access on remote command
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for executables downloaded from known phishing or fake browser update domains. Detect processes that immediately make outbound HTTP POST requests to suspicious infrastructure. Alert on processes that capture screenshots, enumerate installed software via registry, or execute arbitrary commands via cmd.exe /c on remote instruction. Watch for DLLs dropped and executed from %TEMP% using rundll32.exe. Correlate file creation or self-replication in %TEMP% with subsequent suspicious process activity. Combine network, file, and behavioral indicators for high-confidence detection.
